description: We are building MarsWalk Navigator: a web map for astronauts planning a safe walk on Mars. It layers NASA/USGS photo and elevation data of Gale Crater, marks steep ground, and plans a safe route. Looking for help with web design, JavaScript mapping, or Mars science storytelling. First-year CSE students learning as we build. Open to teammates who can join quickly.
summary: Mangal Saarthi (MarsWalk Navigator) is a web-based Martian map that helps plan a safer walk for astronauts on the surface of Mars. We used real NASA and USGS data of Gale Crater, the Curiosity rover's landing region: a HiRISE orthophoto mosaic (25 cm) and a 1 m digital elevation model, which we turned into a 4 m slope grid. The map shows slope hazards (caution above 12 degrees, hazard above 20 degrees; these limits are our own assumptions). Users pick a start and destination, or one of three science stops, and the app finds the safest route using an A* path-finding algorithm that avoids steep ground. It also shows distance, walking time, climb, descent, maximum slope and an elevation profile, and can compare the safest route with the shortest one. NASA Mars Trek MOLA and THEMIS layers give planet-wide context. The tool addresses the challenge by turning Mars data into a simple, Google-Maps-style guide for exploration and safety. Radiation and weather data are planned, not yet included.
details:
What it does: MarsWalk Navigator is a web-based Martian map of Gale Crater that helps plan a safer walk on the surface of Mars. The user picks a start and a destination (or one of three science stops) and the app draws the safest walking route over real NASA and USGS imagery, with a slope hazard map on top.

How it works: We used a 25 cm HiRISE photo mosaic and a 1 m elevation model of the Curiosity landing region. With Python and rasterio we cropped one demo area and converted the elevation data into a 4 m slope grid (148 x 148 cells). Slopes above 12 degrees are marked as caution and above 20 degrees as hazard. These two limits are our own assumptions, not official NASA values. An A* path-finding algorithm in JavaScript then finds a route that avoids hazard cells and strongly penalises steep ground. The user can switch between "Safest" and "Shortest" route and see the trade-off (for example, +99 m longer but max slope 19.5 to 12.5 degrees and caution ground 23.1% to 2.6%). A Route Safety card shows distance, walking time (assuming 2 km/h, our assumption), climb, descent, maximum slope and an elevation profile. The map also includes NASA Mars Trek MOLA and THEMIS layers for planet-wide context, a layers panel, a slope hazard legend and a scale bar.

Benefits and impact: The tool turns raw Mars data into a simple, Google-Maps-style guide that anyone can use. It shows why a longer path can be safer, which supports planning for future surface exploration and makes Mars data easier to understand for students and the public.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet (map), Python with numpy, Pillow and rasterio (data processing), GitHub and Vercel (hosting), Canva (presentation). AI tools (Claude and Antigravity) helped write code and text.

Creativity and design: We combined slope hazards, route finding and a Safest vs Shortest comparison in one lightweight static web app that needs no server and no login.

What we considered and limits: We were honest about what is included. Radiation (Curiosity RAD) and weather (REMS) data are planned but not included in this demo. Science stop positions are approximate and chosen from the photo. The demo covers one small study area, not all of Mars. This was a solo project by Sanchita Dey.
dataRefs: HiRISE colour orthophoto mosaic of Gale Crater (NASA/JPL/University of Arizona, via USGS)
USGS MSL Gale Merged DEM 1 m v3 (Calef and Parker, 2016)
NASA Mars Trek (MOLA global base map)
